claim: You can register a new domain with Route 53. You can also transfer the registration of existing domains from other registrars to Route 53, or transfer a domain registered with Route 53 to another registrar.
question: Can you register domains with Route 53, and transfer registrations in and out?

values.display: you can register it with Amazon Route 53
transfer the registration for existing domains from other registrars to Route 53

evidence.quote: When you want to get a new domain name, such as the **example.com** part of the URL http://example.com, you can register it with Amazon Route 53. You can also transfer the registration for existing domains from other registrars to Route 53 or transfer the registration for domains that you register with Route 53 to another registrar.

claim: When you register a domain with Route 53, the service automatically makes itself the DNS service for the domain. It creates a hosted zone with the same name, assigns four name servers to it, and adds those name servers to the domain.
question: What does Route 53 set up automatically when you register a domain with it?

values.display: the service automatically makes itself the DNS service for the domain
Creates a hosted zone that has the same name as your domain

evidence.quote: When you register a domain with Route 53, the service automatically makes itself the DNS service for the domain. It does the following:
Creates a hosted zone that has the same name as your domain.
Gets the name servers from the hosted zone and adds them to the domain.

claim: If you already registered a domain with another registrar, you can transfer the registration to Route 53, but this is not required to use other Route 53 features.
question: Do you have to transfer a domain registration to Route 53 to use Route 53 DNS?

values.display: This isn't required to use other Route 53 features

evidence.quote: If you already registered a domain name with another registrar, you can transfer the domain registration to Route 53. This isn't required to use other Route 53 features.

claim: The registrar for a domain registered through Route 53 is either Amazon Registrar, Inc. or the registrar associate Gandi.
question: Who is the registrar of a domain that you register through Route 53?

values.display: either Amazon Registrar, Inc. or our registrar associate, Gandi

evidence.quote: The domain registrar is either Amazon Registrar, Inc. or our registrar associate, Gandi.

claim: You do not have to use Route 53 as the DNS service provider for domains registered with Route 53. You can also migrate DNS service to another DNS service provider.
question: Can a domain registered with Route 53 use another DNS service provider?

values.display: You don't have to use Route 53 as the DNS service provider for domains registered with Route 53

evidence.quote: (You can also migrate DNS service to another DNS service provider. You don't have to use Route 53 as the DNS service provider for domains registered with Route 53.)

claim: If your current registrar does not provide paid DNS service, you must migrate DNS service before you transfer the domain. Otherwise the registrar stops providing DNS service when you transfer the domain and the associated websites become unavailable.
question: Why migrate DNS service to Route 53 before transferring a domain registration?

values.display: you need to migrate DNS service before you transfer the domain
the registrar will stop providing DNS service when you transfer your domains

evidence.quote: If you're transferring one or more domain registrations to Route 53, and your current registrar doesn't provide paid DNS service, you need to migrate DNS service before you transfer the domain. Otherwise, the registrar will stop providing DNS service when you transfer your domains. The associated websites and web applications will become unavailable on the internet.

claim: The domain should remain available during the whole DNS migration. If the domain is in use, the migration procedure lets you roll back quickly; for an inactive domain, it could be unavailable for a couple of days.
question: Which Route 53 DNS migration option lets you roll back quickly?

values.display: the first option lets you roll back quickly
your domain should remain available during the entire migration process

evidence.quote: For both options, your domain should remain available during the entire migration process. However, in the unlikely event that there are issues, the first option lets you roll back quickly. With the second option, your domain could be unavailable for a couple of days.

claim: When you migrate DNS service for a domain that is in use, you reproduce your current DNS configuration in Route 53: you create a hosted zone with the same name as your domain and create records in it.
question: What do you create in Route 53 first when you migrate DNS service for an existing domain?

values.display: you create a hosted zone that has the same name as your domain
you reproduce your current DNS configuration in Route 53

qualifiers.scope: DNS migration of a domain in use

evidence.quote: When you migrate DNS service from another provider to Route 53, you reproduce your current DNS configuration in Route 53. In Route 53, you create a hosted zone that has the same name as your domain, and you create records in the hosted zone.

claim: If your current DNS configuration is complex, you can get a zone file from your current DNS provider and import it into Route 53. Not all DNS providers offer zone files.
question: How can you copy a complex DNS configuration into Route 53?

values.display: get a zone file from the current DNS service provider and import it into Route 53

evidence.quote: You can simplify the migration if you can get a zone file from the current DNS service provider and import it into Route 53. (Not all DNS service providers offer zone files.)

claim: Resolvers have cached the name servers of your current DNS provider. To make the migration happen all at once, wait for the old NS TTL, which is two days, to expire after you lower the TTL before you change the name servers.
question: How long do you wait after lowering the NS TTL before you switch name servers for a domain in use?

values.display: wait for two days after you lowered the TTL

qualifiers.scope: DNS migration of a domain in use
qualifiers.condition: when the NS TTL was two days

evidence.quote: To make sure that migrating DNS service to Route 53 happens all at one time, wait for two days after you lowered the TTL.

claim: After you change the name servers, monitor traffic. If traffic slows or stops, change the name servers back to the previous ones and find out what went wrong. If traffic is unaffected, raise the NS TTL back to a higher value.
question: What do you do if traffic slows or stops after you switch a domain to Route 53 name servers?

values.display: change the name servers for the domain back to the previous name servers

qualifiers.scope: DNS migration of a domain in use

evidence.quote: **If the traffic slows or stops** – Use the method provided by the previous DNS service to change the name servers for the domain back to the previous name servers.

claim: Lowering the TTL of the NS record, both with your current DNS service provider and with Route 53, reduces downtime for your domain if you find a problem while migrating DNS to Route 53.
question: Why lower the NS record TTL before migrating DNS to Route 53?

values.display: Lowering the TTL for the NS record
reduces downtime for your domain if you discover a problem

evidence.quote: Lowering the TTL for the NS record, both with your current DNS service provider and with Amazon Route 53, reduces downtime for your domain if you discover a problem while migrating DNS to Route 53.

claim: You can create a hosted zone only for a domain that you have permission to administer.
question: For which domains can you create a hosted zone?

values.display: only for a domain that you have permission to administer

evidence.quote: You can create a hosted zone only for a domain that you have permission to administer.

claim: To delegate a subdomain, you create a hosted zone with the subdomain name, create records in it, and then create an NS record in the parent domain's hosted zone. The NS record name is the subdomain name and its values are the four name servers of the new zone.
question: How do you delegate a subdomain to its own hosted zone?

values.display: hosted zone that has the same name as the subdomain
The NS record name must be the subdomain name

evidence.quote: You create a hosted zone that has the same name as the subdomain that you want to route traffic for, such as acme.example.com.

You create a new NS record in the hosted zone for the domain (example.com). The NS record name must be the subdomain name (acme.example.com), and you specify the four name servers that you got in step 3 as the record values.

claim: When you use a separate hosted zone for a subdomain, you can use IAM permissions to restrict access to that hosted zone. Creating a hosted zone for each subdomain can reduce the number of people who need access to the records of the domain's hosted zone.
question: Why would you give a subdomain its own hosted zone?

values.display: use IAM permissions to restrict access to the hosted zone for the subdomain
multiple subdomains managed by different groups

evidence.quote: When you use a separate hosted zone to route traffic for a subdomain, you can use IAM permissions to restrict access to the hosted zone for the subdomain. If you have multiple subdomains managed by different groups, creating a hosted zone for each subdomain can reduce the number of people who need access to records in the hosted zone for the domain.

claim: When you delegate multiple levels of subdomains, always delegate from the parent zone. Delegations from a grandparent to a child zone might not work at all or work only inconsistently.
question: From which zone should you delegate a sub-subdomain such as www.dept.example.com?

values.display: always delegate from the parent zone
might not work at all or work only inconsistently

evidence.quote: When you delegate multiple levels of subdomains in DNS, it is important to always delegate from the parent zone.
Delegations from a *grandparent* to a *child* zone might not work at all or work only inconsistently.

claim: DNSSEC signing lets DNS resolvers validate that a DNS response came from Route 53 and has not been tampered with. Every response for a signed hosted zone is signed using public key cryptography.
question: What does DNSSEC signing in Route 53 do?

values.display: validate that a DNS response came from Amazon Route 53
every response for a hosted zone is signed using public key cryptography

evidence.quote: Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) signing lets DNS resolvers validate that a DNS response came from Amazon Route 53 and has not been tampered with. When you use DNSSEC signing, every response for a hosted zone is signed using public key cryptography.

claim: In Route 53 DNSSEC signing, each key-signing key (KSK) is based on an asymmetric customer managed key in AWS KMS that you own. You are responsible for KSK management, including rotation. Route 53 manages the zone-signing key (ZSK).
question: Which key does Route 53 use as the key-signing key for DNSSEC, and who manages it?

values.display: each KSK is based on an
ZSK management is performed by Route 53

evidence.quote: There are two kinds of keys in DNSSEC: a key-signing key (KSK) and a zone-signing key (ZSK). In Route 53 DNSSEC signing, each KSK is based on an [asymmetric customer managed key](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/concepts.html#asymmetric-keys-concept) in AWS KMS that you own. You are responsible for KSK management, which includes rotating it if needed. ZSK management is performed by Route 53.

claim: The customer managed key for DNSSEC signing must be in the US East (N. Virginia) Region. It must be an asymmetric customer managed key with the ECC_NIST_P256 key spec, used only for signing and verification.
question: Which Region and key type must the KMS key for Route 53 DNSSEC signing have?

values.display: must be in the US East (N. Virginia) Region
ECC_NIST_P256

evidence.quote: The customer managed key that you use with DNSSEC signing must be in the US East (N. Virginia) Region.

The customer managed key must be an [asymmetric customer managed key](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/symm-asymm-concepts.html#asymmetric-cmks) with an [ECC\_NIST\_P256 key spec](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/asymmetric-key-specs.html#key-spec-ecc). These customer managed keys are used only for signing and verification.

claim: When you enable DNSSEC signing for a hosted zone, Route 53 limits the TTL to one week. If you set a longer TTL you get no error, but Route 53 enforces one week.
question: What happens to a TTL longer than one week in a hosted zone with DNSSEC signing?

values.display: Route 53 limits the TTL to one week

evidence.quote: When you enable DNSSEC signing for a hosted zone, Route 53 limits the TTL to one week. If you set a TTL of more than one week for records in the hosted zone, you don't get an error. However, Route 53 enforces a TTL of one week for the records.

claim: When you use DNSSEC signing, multi-vendor configurations are not supported. White-label name servers must be provided by a single DNS provider.
question: Are multi-vendor DNS configurations supported with Route 53 DNSSEC signing?

values.display: multi-vendor configurations are not supported

evidence.quote: When you use DNSSEC signing, multi-vendor configurations are not supported.

claim: If your parent zone is hosted by a DNS provider that does not support DS queries, then when you enable DNSSEC in the child zone, the child zone becomes unresolvable.
question: What happens if the parent zone's DNS provider does not support DS records and you enable DNSSEC in the child zone?

values.display: the child zone will become unresolvable

evidence.quote: Some DNS providers do not support Delegation Signer (DS) records in their authoritative DNS. If your parent zone is hosted by a DNS provider who does not support DS queries (not setting AA flag in the DS query response), then when you enable DNSSEC in its child zone, the child zone will become unresolvable.

claim: You can enable DNSSEC signing for existing and new public hosted zones.
question: Can you enable DNSSEC signing for private hosted zones?

values.display: DNSSEC signing for existing and new public hosted zones

evidence.quote: Yes. You can enable DNSSEC signing for existing and new public hosted zones.

note: The quote names public hosted zones only; the page states no DNSSEC signing for private hosted zones.

claim: After a hosted zone is deleted, if a new hosted zone is created with the same domain name, Route 53 checks whether the delegation records still point to the deleted zone and, if they do, prevents overlapping name servers from being assigned.
question: How does Route 53 protect against dangling delegation records when a hosted zone is deleted?

values.display: Route 53 will check if the delegation records pointing to the deleted hosted zone are still present
Route 53 will prevent any overlapping name servers from being assigned

evidence.quote: Route 53 protects against the dangling delegation record risk in the case where a hosted zone is deleted. After deletion, if a new hosted zone is being created with the same domain name, Route 53 will check if the delegation records pointing to the deleted hosted zone are still present in the parent domain. If they are, Route 53 will prevent any overlapping name servers from being assigned.

claim: Route 53 cannot protect against every dangling delegation risk. To protect yourself, make sure the parent NS records match the delegation set of the Route 53 hosted zone. Enabling DNSSEC signing adds another layer of protection.
question: What should you do so that parent NS records do not become dangling delegation records?

values.display: make sure the parent NS records match the delegation set
enabling DNSSEC signing for a Route 53 hosted zone can serve as another layer of protection

evidence.quote: To protect yourself against this broader set of risks, make sure the parent NS records match the delegation set for the Route 53 hosted zone.
Additionally, enabling DNSSEC signing for a Route 53 hosted zone can serve as another layer of protection beyond the best practices mentioned above.

claim: If you delegate a domain to Route 53 name servers before a hosted zone exists, Route 53 cannot protect against the dangling delegation. Delegate only to Route 53 name servers that belong to a public hosted zone that you control.
question: Why should you create the hosted zone before you delegate a domain to Route 53 name servers?

values.display: only delegate to Route 53 name servers that belong to a public hosted zone that you control

evidence.quote: To mitigate the risk, only delegate to Route 53 name servers that belong to a public hosted zone that you control.
